title: Node-cache for In-Memory Caching
description: Use node-cache to add fast, time-based in-memory caching directly inside your Node.js process.

data.text: In-memory caching keeps frequently accessed data directly inside your Node.js process, avoiding network round-trips entirely. The `node-cache` package is a popular choice: it is lightweight, has zero runtime dependencies, and supports Time-To-Live (TTL) expiry out of the box. For small-to-medium datasets that fit comfortably in your application heap, node-cache can cut response times from milliseconds down to microseconds.

Every time your application reads data from a database or makes an HTTP request, it pays a latency cost. In-memory caches eliminate that cost for repeated reads of the same data. The trade-off is clear: your cache lives only as long as the Node.js process, so a restart clears the cache. For read-heavy workloads with stable datasets, this trade-off is usually acceptable.

data.title: In-Memory vs Distributed Caching
data.text: Node-cache is process-local. Multiple Node.js instances each maintain their own separate cache. If you need shared state across instances, consider Redis or Memcached instead.
Install `node-cache` via npm or yarn, then create a cache instance with optional defaults. You can set a global TTL and a check-period, which periodically sweeps expired keys.

data.title: When to use node-cache
items: Avoiding repeated calls to slow I/O in the same process

data.title: Memory Limits
data.text: Node-cache stores everything in the V8 heap. Large datasets can trigger garbage collection pauses. Monitor heap usage with --max-old-space-size and profile with clinic.js when needed.

terms.definition: Time-To-Live: the duration after which a cache entry is considered stale and can be evicted.
A read that finds the requested key already in the cache.
A read that does not find the key; the application must fetch from the source and repopulate the cache.

items.question: Should I use node-cache with a Redis instance too?
items.answer: Yes, many teams layer both: node-cache for ultra-fast repeated reads in-process, and Redis as the shared L2 cache.

items.question: Does node-cache support namespacing?
items.answer: Not natively, but prefixing keys (e.g., user:42) achieves the same effect and keeps invalidation predictable.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Node-cache is a zero-dependency, in-process cache for Node.js.
TTL ensures stale entries are evicted automatically.
It is best suited for single-instance applications with small-to-medium datasets.
